item.title: What No One Tells You When the ER Doors Close
item.description:
Depression

What No One Tells You When the ER Doors Close

The discharge papers don't tell you what comes next. Here's the road map.

Posted August 9, 2026

Key points
  • Most people leave a mental health crisis with a phone number list and no real guidance for what to do next.
  • The first 48 hours after discharge are the highest-risk. Having a concrete action plan can change outcomes.
  • Recovery is not linear. Knowing your personal warning signs is as important as intervention itself.

I want to share a moment that is familiar to me.

A patient is stable. The crisis has passed—the overdose treated, a psychiatric hold now completed, the immediate danger contained. Then a nurse hands over discharge papers with a stack of instructions, a few phone numbers, and a referral. The patient and family are instructed to “follow up within a week.” Then the doors open and they walk back into their world.

The hospital’s part in the story is over. But the real healing is just beginning.

I spent more than two decades in emergency medicine. We are trained for the emergency itself. Stabilizing and intervening. We get people through the worst hours of their lives. That is what the ER is built for. What it is not built for is what comes next.

Patients and families leave with very little sense of what the next few days and weeks will actually feel like. The emergency department runs on urgency and focus. Once the immediate danger is handled, attention moves to the next patient. The family standing at the discharge desk is still trying to absorb what all just happened, the patient is still shaken, most don't understand what they are supposed to do now.

That first week after the crisis is where the gap shows itself.

The phone numbers provided on a discharge sheet do not reach a human and go to voicemail. Any available appointment slots are weeks out. Possibly the insurance company brings up requirements nobody explained in the hospital. The first weeks are when we lose progress and support from the initial treatment effort. The patient, even though medically stable, may already be backing away from the follow-up. They can minimize what happened, resist help, insist that they are fine now. The family member trying to help is often left carrying fear, navigating logistics, and facing uncertainty at the same time.

I saw this from the provider side for years. Then there came a time when I saw it from the other side.

My own depression came on slowly; it did not begin in a dramatic crisis. I was still working and still functioning. I was still doing what people expected me to do, while privately losing ground. One day sitting in my car after a shift, I was beaten, unable to start the engine and go home. This feeling at the bottom was a sign of depression closing in. I had recognized them in other people hundreds of times, but had been ignoring them in myself. Knowledge did not make the problems any easier.

What I learned slowly, with more false starts than I would have liked, is that recovery after a mental health crisis is not a single event. It does not end when the patient leaves the hospital or office. It is something that has to be built afterward. This is the area often without much guidance and usually with more uncertainty than the discharge packet suggests.

The gap is real.
Source: Micah & Sammie Chaffin/Unsplash

That is the gap this column is meant to address in many of my posts.

Every post here comes from two places: what I know as a clinician who spent more than two decades treating people in crisis, and what I understand as a patient who had to learn recovery from the inside. It is not inspiration or theory. It is the reality of what happens after the ER doors close and what actually helps people get through those first days. I lived it.

If you are coming out of a crisis, or helping someone who is, this space is for you. Those first days can feel disorienting and lonely. They do not have to stay that way. You are not alone in this. There is a path forward.

If you have been through this as the patient or the person supporting one, share what the hardest part of that first week was that no one prepared you for.

Kenneth Scott Burnham, D.O., is a board-certified emergency physician and the author of LIFELINE: What to Do After a Mental Health Crisis (Guidestone Publishing).
